terms.definition: a model built from many small units (artificial neurons) wired in layers, loosely copied from the brain.
one unit of a neural network: it takes several numbers in and sends one number out.

a brain cell: it receives signals through its branches (dendrites), decides in its cell body whether to fire, and sends its signal along one long fibre (the axon) to other cells through junctions called synapses.
the short electrical pulse a biological neuron sends down its axon when it fires.
a chemical a biological neuron releases at a synapse to pass its signal to the next cell.
a group of neurons that all work on the same input at the same step; a network is a stack of layers.
the cut-off value: a neuron fires (outputs 1) only when its input reaches the threshold.
graphics processing unit: a chip built for games that also does the many multiplications of neural networks very fast.
the best possible solution overall; a local optimum is only the best among nearby solutions.
the rule a neuron applies to its weighted sum to produce its output (step, sigmoid, ReLU, softmax ...).
rectified linear unit, the most common activation: max(0, z) — negative sums become 0, positive ones pass through.
the number on one connection: the input travelling along it is multiplied by it. Training adjusts the weights.
a mathematical stand-in for a brain cell: inputs in, one output out. McCulloch and Pitts' first version used only on/off (1/0) values.
only two possible values: on or off, 1 or 0 (a binary classifier chooses between two classes).
a rule on on/off inputs: AND is on only when both inputs are on; OR when at least one is; NOT flips on and off.
a connection that pushes the receiving neuron toward firing.
a connection that stops (vetoes) the receiving neuron from firing.
exclusive OR: on when exactly ONE of two inputs is on, off when both are on or both are off.
a table listing the output of a logic rule for every combination of inputs.
the 1957 neural network of one layer of threshold logic units; it classifies by drawing a straight boundary.
an artificial neuron that multiplies each input by a weight, adds them up plus a bias, then applies a step function.
multiply each input by its own weight and add the results: w1·x1 + w2·x2 + …
one extra number a neuron adds to its weighted sum; it moves the neuron's threshold. (Not the same as "bias" meaning a systematic error.)
a rule that turns any number into a flat verdict: Heaviside gives 0 below zero and 1 from zero up; sgn gives −1, 0 or +1.
a layer where every input is wired to every neuron (Keras calls it Dense).
all a layer's weights in one table: one row per input, one column per neuron.
the size of each correction step during training: too big and training jumps around, too small and it crawls.
after a wrong prediction, move each weight by learning rate × error × its input; correct predictions change nothing. It follows Donald Hebb's idea that connections used together get stronger.
the line (or surface) where a classifier's answer switches from one class to the other.
the classes can be split by a single straight line (or flat surface).
MLP: a neural network with an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer.
a layer between the input and the output; you never see its values directly.
the training method: a forward pass to predict, a backward pass that works out how much each weight caused the error, then one gradient-descent step on every weight.
one full pass over the training set.
a small group of training instances (32 by default in Keras) used for one training step.
running inputs through the network, layer by layer, to get its predictions.
the single number that says how wrong the predictions were on a batch; training tries to make it smaller.
letting the computer work out every slope (gradient) exactly from the formulas; reverse mode does it for all weights in one backward pass.
the calculus rule for the slope of a function inside another function; it lets the error at the output be traced back to a weight deep inside.
a slope: how fast one quantity changes when another is nudged. ∂L/∂w = how much the loss moves if one weight moves ("partial": all other weights held still).
the S-shaped activation 1 / (1 + e^−z): squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1.
the hyperbolic tangent: an S-shaped activation that squeezes any number into −1 to 1.
signals travel one way only, from inputs to outputs, with no loops back.
the first layer: it just passes the input features in.
the last layer: its neurons produce the network's answers.
here: neurons that start with identical weights stay identical forever, so a layer acts like a single neuron; random starting weights break that symmetry.
an activation log(1 + e^z): near 0 for negative z, near z for positive z, never negative.
a loss that squares small errors (like MSE) but grows only linearly for big ones, so a few wild errors cannot dominate.
mean squared error: square every error and average them (RMSE is its square root).
a popular optimizer that adapts the step size for each weight; it usually works without careful tuning.
the part of training that updates the weights from the gradients (SGD, Adam ...).
Scikit-Learn's ready-made regression MLP.
the smallest rectangle around an object in an image: a centre plus a width and a height.
an output activation for a whole layer: turns raw scores into probabilities between 0 and 1 that add up to exactly 1.
a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is (0.79 = 79% likely).
each instance belongs to exactly one of three or more classes (a digit is 0 or 1 or … 9).
each instance can have several yes/no labels at once (spam AND urgent).
the standard classification loss: small when the model puts a high probability on the correct class, large when it is confidently wrong.
whether predicted probabilities match reality: of all predictions made at 0.9, about 9 in 10 should be right.
the easy-to-use neural-network library inside TensorFlow (tf.keras): layers, models, training loops.
Google's deep-learning library; Keras runs on top of it.
70,000 grey 28 × 28 photos of clothing in 10 classes (T-shirt, trouser … ankle boot); a harder drop-in for the handwritten-digit MNIST.
70,000 grey 28 × 28 photos of handwritten digits 0 to 9 (Chapter 3).
one dot of an image, one number; here 0 (white) to 255 (black).
8-bit unsigned integer: whole numbers from 0 to 255, one byte each.
a number with a decimal point (0.5, 1e-3), as opposed to a whole number.
Meta's deep-learning library, a popular alternative to Keras and TensorFlow; not used in this book.
Keras's simplest way to build a model: a list of layers, each feeding the next.
a layer that reshapes each input grid (28 × 28) into one long row (784 values); it has no weights.
model.summary() prints each layer with its output shape and number of parameters.
NumPy/TensorFlow's rule that adding a row of numbers to a table adds it to every row.
Keras's default way to pick random starting weights, scaled to the layer's size (Chapter 11).
the Keras call that attaches a loss, an optimizer and metrics to a built model, before training.
a number reported during training for you to read (like accuracy); it does not steer the training.
the share of instances a classifier gets right (0.87 = 87%).
class labels stored as one integer per instance (3), as opposed to one-hot vectors; "sparse categorical crossentropy" is the loss for them.
SGD: gradient descent that takes one step per mini-batch, using that batch's gradient; plain SGD with a fixed learning rate.
the POSITION of the largest value (np.argmax) — the index, not the value.
in Keras, the training loop: runs the epochs, one weight update per mini-batch.
how many instances go into one mini-batch (Keras's default: 32).
fit() arguments that make some classes (class_weight) or some instances (sample_weight) count more in the loss.
the object fit() returns; history.history holds one loss and metric value per epoch.
a chart of loss or accuracy against epochs, for training and validation data.
Keras: score the model on some data (loss and metrics), without changing any weight.
an average updated as you go: after each batch, the mean of all batches so far in this epoch.
Keras: run the model on new instances; a classifier returns one probability per class for each.
a minimum probability below which you do not trust the top prediction (and, say, ask a person).
TensorFlow's name for an array of numbers of any number of dimensions.
a Keras layer that standardizes its inputs (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) using statistics measured by adapt().
the call that lets a Keras preprocessing layer measure its statistics (here the means and standard deviations) from the training data.
a number saved with the model that gradient descent does not change (like the Normalization layer's means).
the Keras style where you call each layer on the output of the previous one, so paths can branch and join.
a network with a short (wide) path from inputs to output and a long (deep) path through hidden layers, joined before the output.
a placeholder that describes data (its shape and type) without holding any; calling layers on it only records the wiring.
glue arrays side by side: 5 values and 30 values become one row of 35.
an extra output attached partway through the network, used only during training to guide it.
anything added to training that restricts the model so it overfits less.
a network of steps where links have a direction and nothing ever loops back.
the Keras style where you write your own Python class: layers made in __init__(), the computation written in call().
a Python blueprint for objects; a class can inherit from (build on) another class and reuse its methods.
the method Keras runs on every forward pass of a subclassed model.
declarative = you describe the structure and the tool checks it before running; imperative = you write the steps and find out by running them.
tf.keras.models.clone_model: make a fresh copy of a model's architecture.
TensorFlow's folder format for a trained model: the computation (saved_model.pb) plus every parameter value (variables/).
a single-file format for arrays; the older Keras format uses it.
the running numbers an optimizer like Adam keeps for every weight; saving them lets training resume smoothly.
a copy of the model saved during training, so a crash does not lose the work.
turn an object in memory into bytes that can be written to a file and read back.
an object you give to fit(); Keras calls its methods at fixed moments (end of each epoch, each batch …).
stop training when the validation score has not improved for a while.
EarlyStopping's setting: how many epochs in a row without improvement it tolerates before stopping.
TensorFlow's visual dashboard: a small web server that draws learning curves and more from log files.
the log file TensorBoard reads: training writes a record into it after each epoch.
measuring where the time goes while a program runs, to find the slow part.
a library that searches hyperparameters for Keras models automatically.
the set of all hyperparameter values a search is allowed to try.
one try in a hyperparameter search: one set of values, one trained model, one score.
the part of a Keras Tuner search that decides which hyperparameter values to try next.
spacing values by multiplication instead of addition, so 0.0001–0.001 gets as many tries as 0.001–0.01.
a search strategy that starts many trials with only a few epochs each and keeps training only the most promising ones, so little time goes to weak settings.
a Keras Tuner class you subclass to control both building (build) and training (fit) of each trial's model.
starting a new model from the lower layers of a model already trained on a similar task, instead of from random weights.
levels built on levels: edges make shapes, shapes make objects.
the narrowest point, which limits everything after it: the slowest part of a program, or (b21) a layer so narrow that information is lost there for good.
starting training with a small learning rate and raising it over the first steps.
able to express anything of a kind: any logic rule (b02), or — for a big enough network — any reasonable function; in theory, with no promise about size or training.
a website where you can train tiny neural networks in the browser and watch them learn.
Google's deep-learning library for fast numerical code; not used in this book.
a search strategy that uses the scores of the trials so far to choose the most promising values to try next.
